purpose: Test whether functional recurrence and architectural contingency are island-specific rather than general properties of plant-pollinator mutualisms, and identify the narrower geography-specific signal that survives falsification.

controls.geographic_scope: global wild plants across island and mainland landscapes
controls.source: Bennett et al. 2020 Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-020-17751-y
controls.design: phylogenetically controlled meta-analysis of 2247 study populations and 1247 wild plant species
controls.result: Pollen limitation is globally common and is strongly conditioned by pollinator dependence, ecological specialization and functional specialization; autofertile plants are not pollen limited across land-use categories.
controls.reason: Reproductive dependence on pollination function is a global plant property, not an island-exclusive pattern.

controls.geographic_scope: 52 quantitative networks: 18 oceanic islands, 23 continental islands, 11 mainlands
controls.source: Traveset et al. 2016 Global Ecology and Biogeography, doi:10.1111/geb.12362
controls.design: generalized mixed-model comparison controlling for region, sampling intensity, latitude and network size
controls.result: Continental-island networks are broadly similar to mainland networks, whereas oceanic-island networks are smaller, topologically simplified, lower in interaction diversity and higher in plant niche overlap.
controls.reason: The strongest geography-specific signal lies in oceanic-island network structure rather than in pollination function itself.

controls.source: Magrach et al. 2017 Nature Ecology & Evolution, doi:10.1038/s41559-017-0249-9
controls.design: field study linking honeybee spillover, pollinator-network reorganization and wild-plant reproductive success
controls.result: Honeybee spillover reshuffles pollinator diets/network structure and translates into a negative reproductive effect on a dominant wild plant.
controls.reason: Interaction reorganization with reproductive consequences also occurs on mainlands.

controls.source: Wang et al. 2024 Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-024-52465-5
controls.design: field experiments on pollinator communities, interactions and wild-plant reproductive performance
controls.result: A dominant-pollinator shift from flies to honeybees reconfigures interactions and can increase, decrease or leave unchanged reproductive success depending on plant species.
controls.reason: Species-specific functional consequences of partner replacement are not unique to islands.

controls.geographic_scope: 40 coastal networks across Japanese continental and oceanic islands; 8 sites x 5 seasons
controls.design: natural gradient analysis of pollinator functional diversity, trait matching and pollination success in 10 plant species
controls.result: Pollinator species richness, functional evenness, functional diversity and community-level trait matching decreased with distance from the continental main island; lower community-level trait matching reduced plant pollination success regardless of flower morphology.
controls.reason: This supplies a direct geography-to-functional-architecture-to-pollination-function pathway, but it is one regional natural experiment and requires independent replication.

controls.geographic_scope: Wanshan continental island versus Yongxing oceanic island, China
controls.source: Wang et al. 2025 Biotropica, doi:10.1111/btp.70027; Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.t76hdr8bj
controls.design: community and co-occurring-plant comparison of species composition, network structure and pollinator importance
controls.result: Highly dissimilar species composition produced strongly different network structures; the oceanic network had higher connectance, nestedness, specialization and plant niche overlap, while co-occurring plants had lower pollinator richness and visitation than on the continental island.
controls.reason: A recent independent continental-oceanic comparison replicates strong architecture change even among co-occurring plant species.

refined_repository_claim: Pollination dependence and architectural contingency are general mutualism biology rather than island-specific discoveries. The surviving island-biogeographic signal is a constraint shift: oceanic insularity changes the partner and link opportunity space, and at least one natural continental-oceanic gradient shows that this loss/reorganization of functional interaction space propagates through trait matching to pollination success.
candidate_new_synthesis: constraint-mediated functional conservation: reproductive function is generic, while oceanic isolation alters the feasible interaction architecture through which that function can be maintained; floral and reproductive responses are then conditional solutions to that constrained architecture rather than a universal island syndrome.
next_test: Seek independent oceanic-versus-continental/mainland systems with both source-native architecture metrics and reproductive-performance measures, then test whether geography modifies architecture-to-function coupling without pooling incompatible estimands.
claim_boundary: The current evidence does not yet establish a globally stronger architecture-function coupling on oceanic islands, nor that architecture causes floral divergence. Hiraiwa 2024 is direct but regional; Traveset 2016 and Wang 2025 independently establish geography-architecture differences without the same reproductive endpoint.
